title: ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Hits Nearly 19 Billion Minutes Viewed, Most-Watched Streaming Series of the Summer
description:
“Love Island USA” is officially the series of the summer.

	According to Peacock, Season 8 of the reality dating series has reached nearly 19 billio
body:
“Love Island USA” is officially the series of the summer.

	According to Peacock, Season 8 of the reality dating series has reached nearly 19 billion minutes watched to date, spanning 35 episodes released between June 2 and July 13 — making it the streamer’s most-watched original season ever. Divided by the season’s nearly 40-hour runtime, that total translates to an estimate of close to 7.9 million views.


	First-party data also indicates that 30% of the seasons’ viewership came from phones and tablets, one of Peacock’s biggest mobile audiences ever. Additionally, 35% of viewers were new to the series, not having watched previous seasons, and nearly half of viewers watched the series with at least one other person. And “Aftersun,” Peacock’s “Love Island” aftershow hosted by Ciara Miller and Tefi Pessoa saw a 135% increase compared to last season.
	

	By Nielsen’s measure, “Love Island USA” Season 8 is the most-watched streaming series of summer  2026 in addition to being the No. 1 streaming reality title for six consecutive weeks. These superlatives were calculated based on data measured between May 25 and July 12; Nielsen operates on a multi-week delay for streaming titles.

	Unsurprisingly, the season has been a phenomenon on social media. Per Social Content Ratings, it generated more than 5 billion video views across platforms, and more than 2.5 billion views came from TikTok — marking a 47% increase from Season 7 and accounting for 68% of Season 8’s total social engagement. 

	On the “Love Island USA” app, where viewers can vote on multiple outcomes including which contestants get to stay on the show, there was an 85% increase in users and a 35% increase in voters compared to Season 7. Both the show’s app and the Peacock app reached No. 1 on the App Store during the run of Season 8.
	

	News of “Love Island” Season 8’s ratings success comes ahead of the reunion special on Aug. 31, which will be hosted by Ariana Madix and Andy Cohen on Peacock.

	“Love Island USA” is produced by ITV America in association with Lifted Entertainment and WPP Media Company’s Motion Entertainment. ITV Studios distributes the series. Executive producers include David George, Adam Sher, Jordana Hochman, Bernie Schaeffer, Ben Thursby-Palmer, James Barker, Blake Garrett, Courtney Rosenthal, Sophie Brown, Jessica Castro, Richard Cowles, Mike Spencer, Tom Gould, Chet Fenster and Martin Oxley.

schema.headline: ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Hits Nearly 19 Billion Minutes Viewed, Most-Watched Streaming Series of the Summer

title: Bella Thorne and Zendaya Got Pitted Against Each Other During Disney Fame and Snuck Off Set to ‘Hash It Out’ After Things ‘Got Pretty Bad’
description: Bella Thorne revealed on the latest episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast that she was aggressively pitted against her “Shake It Off” co-star Zend
body:
Bella Thorne revealed on the latest episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast that she was aggressively pitted against her “Shake It Off” co-star Zendaya amid the height of their Disney stardom. The two actors became household names among Disney Channel viewers for playing CeCe Jones (Thorne) and Rocky Blue (Zendaya) on “Shake It Off,” which ran for three seasons and 75 episodes between 2010 and 2013.

	“With women it’s like, ‘We have to make you all beg for one spot… if you can beat each other down and scrap to whatever extent we’re asking you two [and] eat yourselves alive while we have all these spots but for women, it’s just one of you…’ The patriarchy has been doing it since the beginning of time,” Thorne recalled. “You go back and we were 12! What’s wrong with you? We are supposed to be best friends. We play best friends. It got pretty bad.”
	

	The situation at Disney got so bad that one day while filming an episode Thorne and Zendaya snuck off so they could be alone together and have a heart-to-heart about the situation.


	“It got to a point where when we were on our ‘Good Luck Charlie’ crossover, we escaped to another set in the middle of live taping — which is really ballsy, badass and rebellious. We snuck out. We knew we had three scenes until we were up again and we like just went to talk,” Thorne said. “We got into it, hashed it out, and it was so beautiful” 

	“It was my first experience — woman to woman, girl to girl — where you actually can speak,” she added. “You can both be heard about the different things you’ve been experiencing and what people are saying and how they’re trying to do this to you. You can walk out of there seeing each other… It was one of the most genuine girl-on-girl talks.”
	

	Thorne and Zendaya have been honest in the past about how being pitted against each other threatened to derail their friendship. The former told Us Weekly in 2021 that “all of a sudden everyone is pitting you against each other and that fed into our heads. It made us not [be] friends in that first season.”

	Watch Thorne’s full interview on “Call Her Daddy” in the video below.

title: Judge Dismisses Lawsuit From Paramount Streaming Subscribers Seeking to Block Warner Bros. Merger
description: A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed a lawsuit from a group of consumers looking to challenge the $111 billion merger between Paramount and Warner
body:
A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed a lawsuit from a group of consumers looking to challenge the $111 billion merger between Paramount and Warner Bros.

	Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín wrote that the plaintiffs — three current Paramount+ subscribers and two prospective subscribers — presented a lack of standing in their suit. She also ruled that the plaintiffs failed to establish “cognizable” economic fallout that would invoke antitrust regulation. However, she has allowed plaintiffs to revise their complaint and refile.
	

	“The Complaint contains a boilerplate assertion of competitive harms, such as ‘lower quality and variety’ and ‘decreased consumer choice,’ but it fails to allege any facts to plausibly show how those claimed harms have materialized or would materialize,” she wrote. She later added, “Plaintiffs’ standing theory amounts to little more than the assertion that they are consumers who watch television and go to the movies, and therefore a merger between Entertainment companies would injure them.”


	Judge Martínez-Olguín will also preside over the antitrust cases from a group of 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America, which both claim the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger will do irreparable harm to the entertainment industry. Those cases are set for trial on March 2, 2027.

	Paramount-Skydance CEO David Ellison recently published an op-ed in The New York Times, in which he wrote that the reason the state AGs want the merger blocked is not because of consolidation, but because he will control CNN if he’s allowed to scoop up Warner Bros. Ellison’s ties to President Donald Trump, a long time critic of CNN, and the recent troubles with “60 Minutes” have made some in Hollywood nervous about the future of the historic news network.
	

	“I believe this fight is not really about market share,” Ellison wrote. “I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN.” Ellison, reasserting his goal of an independent CNN, added, “When it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth.”

schema.headline: Judge Dismisses Lawsuit From Paramount Streaming Subscribers Seeking to Block Warner Bros. Merger

title: Music Industry Moves: Alicia Keys Signs With CAA in All Areas; SONA’s Emerging Songwriter Award Nominations Now Open
description:
Alicia Keys has signed with CAA in all areas, the company announced earlier this week. 

	Among her many achievements, the singer-songwriter has sol
body:
Alicia Keys has signed with CAA in all areas, the company announced earlier this week. 

	Among her many achievements, the singer-songwriter has sold an estimated 65 million records since the release of her 2001 debut album, “Songs in A Minor,” and is the subject of “Hell’s Kitchen,” a Broadway musical featuring her music and lyrics inspired by her life growing up in New York in the 1990s. It won two Tony Awards amid 13 nominations and a 2025 Grammy for Best Musical Theater Album. She is also a founding member of She Is the Music, a nonprofit to advance women’s careers in music. She is managed by Roc Nation; she had previously been with WME for nearly 15 years.
	

	+ Songwriters of North America has announced that nominations for the 2026 Emerging Songwriter Award, presented by YouTube Songwriters, are now open. According to the announcement, the award “uplifts a SONA member who exemplifies originality, craft, and a commitment to creative integrity.”


	Five finalists — who must be SONA members to be considered — will be recognized, with the recipient announced live at the Annual SONA Awards on Thursday, October 29, 2026, at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles, California. Songwriter must have at least three publicly released songs in the past two years and at least three outside cuts (songs cut by another artist).

	Nominations are open through Friday, August 14, 2026. The finalists and winner will be decided by the SONA membership. Finalists will receive a package which includes priority invitations to YouTube events like writing camps and masterclasses, dedicated strategy sessions with the YouTube team, SONA and YouTube curated stewardship with SONA Award nominees and winners, the opportunity to perform at select SONA events, and more.
	

	“SONA has always been built on a simple idea: by Songwriters, for Songwriters. That’s what makes this award, created in partnership with YouTube Songwriters and voted on by SONA members, so meaningful. It’s Songwriters celebrating Songwriters, and recognizing the incredible new voices shaping what comes next,” said Michelle Lewis, SONA Co-Founder and CEO of SONA and the SONA Foundation.

	“It is incredibly exciting to watch this award continue to take shape now in its second year, further cementing YouTube Music and SONA’s shared commitment to championing songwriters at every step of their journey,” said Jenna Rubenstein, Head of Songwriter Relations for YouTube Music. “We are honored to keep shining a light on the songwriting community’s immense talent, and it remains deeply meaningful that this award comes directly from fellow songwriters who intimately know the soul of this work.”

	+ Prescription Songs has signed Nashville-based producer-songwriter-engineer Rich Harris, who has worked closely with SZA, DJ Khaled and Sexyy Red, among others, as well as commercial work. The signing was led by A&Rs Chris Martingago and Sophia Battaglia, in partnership with Pray for My Haters, a venture founded by producer-songwriter Tony Esterly and manager Dave Hopper.

	“This is the dream team!” Harris said. “I’m very grateful to be working with a group of people that so personally understands my work and operates with such intention. Everyone on this crew has already been pushing hard for me and I couldn’t be more excited to have made this official.”

	+ The Country Music Association has announced the newest class of participants into its Women’s Leadership Academy, after a record year of applicants, according to the announcement. The academy kicked off with an opening reception on August 2, at the Chloe Nashville, where Sarah Trahern, CMA Chief Executive Officer, and Tiffany Kerns, Senior Vice President of Industry Relations and Philanthropy, delivered opening remarks.

	“Over the next 12 weeks, the cohort-based program will guide 16 high-performing, high-potential women through weekly group coaching, peer connection, and hands-on leadership training,” the announcement reads. “Beyond learning directly from executive coaches and industry mentors, participants join a growing community of program alumni who continue supporting one another well beyond the program’s conclusion.”
	

	“Every new class of the Women’s Leadership Academy reminds me how much talent and heart exist in this industry,” says Kerns. “This program was built to outlast its 12 weeks. The relationships, confidence and perspective these women gain stay with them well beyond the program. Watching this cohort step into the program with such openness and ambition has been inspiring, and I know they’ll carry that same spirit forward as they help define what’s next for our business.”

	The new class of CMA’s Women’s Leadership Academy includes:

	Elisabeth Ashley (Manager)

	Kelly Bolton (Vice President, A&R, Warner Records)

	Victoria Cappelli Greiner (Senior Director of Digital Marketing, Global Touring, AEG Presents)

	Annie Flook (Vice President, Artist Relations, AXS)

	Hannah Galluzzi (Vice President, A&R, MCA)

	Claire Heinichen (Senior Editor, Country, Spotify)

	Lindsay Hyslop (Director of Recorded Music, Canada, BMG)

	Lucia Kaminsky (President, The Sandbox)

	Marne McLyman (Manager, Maverick Nashville)

	Kelsey Middleton (Head of Marketing & Digital Strategy, TRACK mgmt)

	Amanda Quinton (President, Quinton Digital)

	Alexis Rosenberg (Head of External Relations, WME)

	Jamie Sudhalter (Head of A&R, The Core Entertainment)

	Randi Tolbert (Senior Artist Manager, Q Prime South)

	Margaret Tomlin (Vice President, A&R, Sony Music Nashville)

	Jamie Lynn Younger (Vice President, Marketing, Big Loud)

title: Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna Backs Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Says Antitrust Trial ‘Creates More Uncertainty and Distraction’
description:
Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna released a statement on Wednesday evening in support of the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. merger. 

	“This year has
body:
Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna released a statement on Wednesday evening in support of the looming Paramount-Warner Bros. merger. 

	“This year has been an important one for our industry. Attendance is up, younger audiences are coming out in numbers we haven’t seen in years, and the upcoming release schedule looks just as strong,” Acuna wrote. “While there is real momentum, we need a thriving studio system to ensure that the industry has a platform from which to grow.”
	

	“This is why, after much consideration, we believe it’s time for Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to move forward,” Acuna continued. The CEO explained that he spoke to Paramount-Skydance CEO David Ellison, who has made “some specific commitments” to ensure the theater business continues to thrive. Those commitments include, “At least 30 theatrical films a year, a protected theatrical window with 45 days for TVOD and 90 days for SVOD for a minimum of three years, and a $30 billion annual investment in media content.”


	“A long fight in court that extends into spring or summer doesn’t put more films in theaters, and is not beneficial to studios, filmmakers, the guests who go to the movies, or theater businesses like Regal and the people who work for them,” Acuna added. “It just creates more uncertainty and distraction that could be damaging to our industry as we build on our current success.”

	Regal’s backing comes a week after AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron published an op-ed in Variety explaining his own reasons for supporting the deal. With the addition of Regal, Ellison now has the country’s two largest theater chains on his side, which will prove to be key allies as he prepares for a March 2027 antitrust showdown against California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs.
	

	The development is a blow to the states’ lawsuit, which was filed on July 13. It alleges that the $111 billion merger violates the Clayton Act by diminishing competition in three key markets: wide-release theatrical distribution, “top-grossing” theatrical distribution and basic cable licensing. The suit also claims the wallets of theater owners and consumers will be hurt if Paramount and Warner Bros. are allowed to merge. However, with AMC and Regal now in the Ellison camp, it will most likely be extremely difficult for Bonta and his team to prove that the exhibition will suffer in a post-merger industry.

	Acuna and Aron also appear to be at odds with Cinema United, the exhibition industry trade group, and its head, Michael O’Leary, who have come out swinging against the sale of Warner Bros. to Paramount. Last week, O’Leary reaffirmed the group’s opposition in a letter to its members, writing, “this transaction will result in fewer movies, higher costs for you and your patrons, and ultimately, fewer theatres. The promises of support for theatrical being made in the media are high-level and unenforceable and as such do nothing to alleviate the harms.”

	On Tuesday, Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a ruling that the antitrust trial will last 12 days, running from March 2, 2027, to March 19. In a July 31 motion, Paramount requested the judge schedule the trial in November, while the states and the Writers Guild of America, who are also suing to stop the merger, requested the trial take place in March. Paramount wants this deal done as soon as possible, considering that it has to pay a “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. Discovery of $7 million for every day past Oct. 1 that the deal remains in limbo. 

	Ellison published an op-ed in the New York Times on Tuesday, in which he wrote that the real reason the state AGs want these deals blocked is that he will control CNN if he’s allowed to scoop up Warner Bros.

	“I believe this fight is not really about market share,” Ellison wrote in the essay. “I believe a plainer worry sits beneath the briefs and the news releases: the news. The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN.” Ellison, reasserting his promise of an independent and fair CNN, added, “When it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth.”
	

	Deadline was the first to report Acuna’s statement backing the merger.

schema.headline: Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna Backs Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Says Antitrust Trial ‘Creates More Uncertainty and Distraction’

title: ‘Super Troopers 3’ Review: A Cult Comedy Franchise Seeks No Converts in Instantly Forgettable Third Go-Round
description: 2018’s “Super Troopers 2” wasn’t so much fan service as fan self-service. Kickstarted with nearly $5 million of crowdfunding after studios doubted t
body:
2018’s “Super Troopers 2” wasn’t so much fan service as fan self-service. Kickstarted with nearly $5 million of crowdfunding after studios doubted the public appetite for a tardy sequel to the 2001 indie sleeper “Super Troopers,” it gave the people what they wanted and not much else: a familiar rehash of the first film’s broad characters and jokes, with a built-in hit of generational nostalgia courtesy of nothing more than time itself. 17 years separated those films; eight years later, along comes “Super Troopers 3,” and any semblance of event status feels duly halved. “Super Troopers 2” wasn’t very good, but its very existence was a satisfying underdog story in itself; made in less time with less resistance from studio brass, the new, Disney-backed film has a more routine, less victorious air of franchise maintenance about it.
	

	For die-hard faithfuls of this proudly lunkheaded series, that might be enough. Continuing the misadventures of its core quintet of inept, resplendently mustachioed Vermont state troopers — played, as ever, by the five individuals making up the Broken Lizard comedy troupe, who also take a collective writing credit — “Super Troopers 3” isn’t obviously a step down from their last outing. The jokes are still wildly scattershot and frequently, knowingly lame; the production is still cheap and cheerfully scrappy; the whole ragged enterprise is still reliant on the evident affection and chemistry between its players to hold it together. None of that really amounts to a persuasive reason to exist on the big screen, however: At this point, perhaps simply turning “Super Troopers” into a running sitcom, like a rural GenX “Brooklyn Nine-Nine,” would be a fitting move.
	

	Not much has changed in the fictional backwoods town of Spurbury, Vermont, and its chaotic highway patrol department: Though gruff former captain O’Hagen (Brian Cox) has officially retired, replaced by the earnestly politically correct Markowski (Nat Faxon), he still hangs around the office in stubborn denial of that fact. His erstwhile team of troopers, meanwhile, are all pushing sixty but staunchly refusing to grow up, as they spend their days joyriding in their patrol cars and pranking passing motorists. Juvenile rookie Coy (“SNL” star Andrew Dismukes) seems to fits right in, and if it weren’t for his TikTok fixation, you’d scarcely notice the age gap. 

	Meanwhile, the running frenemy dynamic between senior trooper Thorny (Chandrasekhar) and his coarse, obnoxious colleague Farva (Kevin Heffernan) takes more strain than usual when Farva becomes engaged to Thorny’s sister Sarita (Hannah Simone). Cue a bonanza of elaborate Indian-American wedding preparations, with the troopers eagerly if unhelpfully assisting in the festivities — save for Thorny, who agrees to be Farva’s best man only so he can sabotage the nuptials from the inside. That “Super Troopers 3” has resorted to standard wedding-farce shenanigans, somewhat awkwardly grafted onto its usual cop antics, suggests a certain dearth of ideas on the script front. It does, at least, allow for some mildly amusing culture-clash comedy centered on Thorny’s not-so-traditional Hindu parents, gamely played by Sakina Jaffrey and Iqbal Theba.

	A secondary narrative involving the troopers’ bumbling attempts to crack a nefarious Canadian drug ring is pretty thin gruel, necessitating a lot of unfunny business about electric cars and maple syrup, devised to keep the other three Broken Lizard members occupied while imminent brothers-in-law Thorny and Farva hash things out. None of them really gets prime material to work with, but then there isn’t a lot of that to go around anyway. Though the film devises a handful of elaborate grossout setpieces — bottoming out, so to speak, with Thorny fisting a wedding elephant — the most immediately funny gags here are often the most benignly stupid and disposable: This critic laughed out loud at the reference to an Indian clothes shop called Turban Outfitters, but repeating the joke certainly doesn’t do much for it.
	

	Then again, one wouldn’t have thought repeating “Super Troopers” a particularly good idea — least of all twice — but a whole quarter of a century later, here we are. “Super Troopers 2” made a solid $32 million at the box office, but it still feels a stretch to describe this second sequel as existing by popular demand: Chandrasekhar and the guys are surely just amusing themselves at this point, confident that their cult will chuckle along with them.

schema.headline: ‘Super Troopers 3’ Review: A Cult Comedy Franchise Seeks No Converts in Instantly Forgettable Third Go-Round

title: ‘Mustache’ Review: A Delightfully Anxious Pakistani American Coming-of-Age Comedy
description: American coming-of-age comedies rarely beat with such uncomfortable verisimilitude. In the bilingual “Mustache” — the first feature from writer-dire
body:
American coming-of-age comedies rarely beat with such uncomfortable verisimilitude. In the bilingual “Mustache” — the first feature from writer-director Imran J. Khan — 13-year-old Pakistani American high schooler Ilyas (Atharv Verma) undergoes an awkward adjustment from a private Islamic institution to a generic American high school. The story’s universality is born from its cultural specificity, as a mid-‘90s tale of a Bay Area outsider, who feels alien both in his social life as well as at home.
	

	Bitingly funny in its comedy and wistful in its drama, the film rests on the delicate performance of newcomer Verma, a diminutive, age-appropriate actor who molds Ilyas in captivating ways. He seems consistently exhausted, both physically and emotionally, and he can only contextualize the world’s unspoken social contracts through careful diagrams and flowery voiceover. These narrations are descriptive, verbose, and imaginative — Ilyas may as well be a sci-fi writer, given his love of “Back to the Future” — but the character seldom has the opportunity (or the confidence) to let his spoken dialogue be as poetic.


	This disconnect of mood and behavior is exacerbated when his immigrant father Hameed (Rizwan Manji), who’s struggling with his new business and has five mouths to feed, pulls Ilyas out of the relative comfort of his San Jose’s community’s Islamic school and transfers him to a local public institution. Leaving behind his classroom crush Yasmeen (Ayana Manji), though staying in touch with her through instant messenger, Ilyas embarks on a clumsy odyssey through mainstream Americana, while concocting ploys to get his parents to re-transfer him back to the relative comforts of his Quranic study. A scrawny kid with a quiet disposition, he’s still a target of bullying either way — but at least this way, he won’t feel like as much of an ethnic anomaly.
	

	The film begins with the religious question of whether young Ilyas is allowed to shave the bristles on his upper lip, leading to a consistent self-consciousness, which appears (and re-appears) as Ilyas imagining extreme close-ups of hair and skin. This hyper-awareness rears its head in moments the otherwise invisible tween is placed under a spotlight by his peers, resulting in quick bursts of visual energy that intentionally get on your nerves.

	That Ilyas is whip-smart for a kid, but extremely reserved, is the fulcrum for much of the comedy. His harebrained schemes to get his parents to believe he’s been “corrupted” by American life — like bringing home McDonald’s and sheepishly eating it in the family kitchen — might even work if they were better executed. All he needs is a partner in crime. He eventually finds one in Yasmeen, who, through numerous IM conversations, ends up writing him emails from a fake girlfriend at his new school, in the hopes that his parents will stumble upon this alleged relationship on the family computer.

	Complicating matters (and turning “Mustache” into a less perverse “Dear Evan Hansen”) is the fact that these emails are based on Ilyas’s real classmate, the witty and attractive Liz Park (Melody Cao), for whom he develops actual feelings after following her to the school’s drama class, led by the kind and helpful Miss Martin (Alicia Silverstone). Soon, an entirely new social life begins to blossom, which runs counter to Ilyas’s scheme to get re-transferred.

	This places Ilyas in an even more awkward situation, as the ball gets rolling on his deception. His chats with Yasmeen — which, although typed out on the internet, are depicted as playful face-to-face conversations by computer-light — become the origin for an impending avalanche of un-truths, threatening to crush whatever momentary bliss he’s able to construct, in a world where finding himself is the ultimate challenge.

	The film ends up with raucously funny situations buoyed by piercing second-hand embarrassment. But all the while, Verma grounds this social chaos in a performance of genuine anxiety spirals, allowing the movie’s minor stakes to feel apocalyptic. Should Ilyas’ ploys become known — akin to Ilyas himself being known, and being completely seen — the result would be social suicide.
	

	Although the movie eventually loses steam (a side effect of its subversions of the genre, while using Ilyas’s awkward outsidership as an aesthetic North Star), Khan traces the care with which his characters try to chart invisible social lines. He does so by employing careful reaction shots, trusting each young performer to quietly establish the stakes and consequences of simple decisions — like Ilyas leaving a similarly-ostracized South Asian peer to go hang out with the “cool kids.” This yields not only hilarious tightrope walks at every turn, but an organic rhythm, where so many other movies of this kind play like forced retrospectives attempting to conjure hazy memories long-forgotten.

	“Mustache,” on the other hand, places its audience painfully front and center, to moments that are so deeply felt and lived-in, you can’t help but laugh at the honest absurdity. It’s like gazing into a mirror that reflects back at your most naked and vulnerable self.

schema.headline: ‘Mustache’ Review: A Delightfully Anxious Pakistani American Coming-of-Age Comedy

title: ‘Soulm8te’ Review: Fembot Goes Rogue in Polished but Predictable Tech Thriller
description: Billed as a spun-off third entry in the “M3GAN” franchise, “Soulm8te” is to “Fatal Attraction” as M3GAN’s vehicles were to “Orphan” and “The Bad See
body:
Billed as a spun-off third entry in the “M3GAN” franchise, “Soulm8te” is to “Fatal Attraction” as M3GAN’s vehicles were to “Orphan” and “The Bad Seed” — a robotic replay of very familiar genre tropes. Here, a grieving widower working in tech agrees to try out a prototype of the titular “AI companion,” basically a beauteous virtual assistant ready to serve all his household, emotional and horizontal needs. You know where this is headed: Robo-lover will grow possessive towards its “master,” then turn into an Unstoppable Killing Machine. 
	

	None of this is remotely credible, or particularly suspenseful. But it is handled with reasonable aplomb by director Kate Dolan and her cast, who do their best to elevate material that can only be raised so far. Universal opted to bypass theatrical release, releasing to digital platforms in the U.S. and several other territories on August 1st. It’s sure to travel the globe as a viable commercial item, though it’s unlikely to stir enthusiasm sufficient to warrant its own sequel. 


	David (David Rysdahl) has worked from home for the last year, cloistered in mourning for the wife who died after a long illness. But when his smaller company is bought up by Ultima Robotix, everyone gets hauled back into the office, where incoming boss Ben (Arty Froushan) shows off the “newest product” they’ll be primarily working on: Soulm8te, a female android targeting economically privileged sectors of the “loneliness epidemic.” (Which is assumed to be entirely male, and heterosexual — at least no equivalent models are being designed for other demographics, yet.) 
	

	Getting pushed out in the merger is old boss Terrence (Elijah Cook), who commiserates at a going-away party that night with Aubrey (Claudia Doumit), the coworker David has a potential romantic frisson with. But Ben has already detected David’s vulnerability, and seems inclined to exploit it. He urges David to download and utilize an app that’s like a personalized, voice-only virtual emotional-support pal. Once hooked on that, it’s a short leap to lending “her” physical form by agreeing to test-drive his very own Soulm8te, whom he dubs Sara (Lily Sullivan). 

	This runway-ready glamazon cooks, cleans, intuits his feelings and offers every kind of, er, relief. Far from a blank slate, she seems to come with a very full encyclopedia of knowledge and skills. After a few hours watching TV, she’s also absorbed every bad commonplace about gender relations, from neurosis about diet and looks to “Jerry Springer”-type combativeness. We’re meant to think that sped-up media education, plus some programming tweaks David makes himself, explain her subsequent aberrant behavior. 

	But Sara is never convincing as a machine. Like numerous similar thrillers before it, this one gives her so many petulant, peculiar and scheming characteristics right away, the central conceit that she’s non-human fails. And it does so long before she goes full Glenn Close, jealously imperiling anyone who might come between her and David. The whole sci-fi pretense evaporates once this screenplay sallies into stock “psycho ex-girlfriend” terrain. 

	Irish writer-director Dolan’s 2021 debut feature “You Are Not My Mother” was an interesting if uneven stab at balancing supernatural horror themes with a serious take on mental illness, played out between three generations of women in a bleak North Dublin housing estate. But this U.S. production (also shot in Ireland, albeit passing as an unspecified American city) does not reach for psychological complexity or nuance. Its screenplay, which Dolan hatched in collaboration with three others, tries to soft-pedal predictable beats that nonetheless end up the only ones getting beaten. 

	Rysdahl and Doumit do make their generically-written characters seem pleasantly relatable. Sullivan has an impossible role that demands a lot without providing much inner logic to ground the performance. In the end, “Sara” is just another in a long screen line of quipping, grinning homicidal sexpots, complete with a sequence in which she actually shags someone to death. If Sara has been programmed only to love and be needed, why does she go violently berserk? The answer, of course: Because this is that kind of movie. 
	

	And for that kind of movie, it’s slickly shot and paced, so that implausibility doesn’t particular hinder the plot’s uncomplicated progress, or the unspectacular but efficient mayhem wreaked. Dolan and her collaborators do a good job smoothing over the presentation of a fairly janky, formulaic concept, to results that are entertaining enough. But all concerned deserve better material to work with, and “Soulm8te” does not raise expectations that the “M3GAN” universe will aim any higher than competent but disposable genre fodder.

schema.headline: ‘Soulm8te’ Review: Fembot Goes Rogue in Polished but Predictable Tech Thriller

title: ‘The Shards’ Star Igby Rigney on Wooing Ryan Murphy, Never Meeting Bret Easton Ellis and Not Worrying About Sex Scenes: ‘It’s Like Doing a Dance Under a Microscope’

body:
Igby Rigney is exhausted. 

	It’s a day before “The Shards” launches, and he’s just gotten back from Berlin, the final stop of a global press tour that also took him to New York and London. When the series debuts on FX on Aug. 5, he’ll be celebrating at the official launch party at a roller rink in Los Angeles. 

	Right now, during this brief moment of calm, he’s home in L.A. and resting with his cat, Plusha, who meows throughout our Zoom interview. “I feel like a Bond villain,” he says, petting the animal in his lap.
	

	Rigney plays Bret in “The Shards,” Ryan Murphy’s adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ 2023 autofiction opus that follows the author in his high school years. Bret navigates teenage social politics, the drug-fueled excesses of 1980s Los Angeles and his closeted homosexuality, all while a serial killer stalks the Valley and picks off his classmates in an increasingly gruesome fashion.


	The series marks the first time the 26-year-old actor headlines a major project. “They asked if I wanted to see the reviews when they come in. I guess they’ll put them in a packet,” Rigney says. “I was like, ‘Oh man, do I? I don’t know.’ I think I said, ‘Yes, I’ll take the packet, but I can’t promise to read all of them.’”
	
		Ryan Murphy said at the New York premiere that about 500 actors auditioned for “The Shards.” What was your audition process like?	

	Yeah, I got the sides in my inbox, and I was super excited because they asked me to come in person to a studio in L.A. for the initial read. That’s very special, because so many times you don’t even get into the room with people until chemistry reads. I was over the moon to be doing it the old-fashioned way — getting to go in, meet the casting director and build a tape together with someone who knows exactly what they’re looking for.
	

	We had a ton of fun in the room. Ryan saw that tape, and asked me to come to New York. That’s where I met [future co-stars] Graham [Campbell] and Hayes [Warner] at that initial callback with Ryan. I came in, and Ryan asked, “Have you read the book?” I was like, “No… I haven’t.” I think I gave a reasonable answer: I was so enamored by the sides he’d written, and I knew this was ultimately going to be an adaptation, so I wanted to focus on the material at hand for the audition. He said, “Great, that was awesome. I’d love to see you again, but go read the book. You must read the book before I see you next.”

	So I did. I actually listened to the audiobook, which is read by Bret. Then I came back in and did a chem read with Graham and a chem read with Homer [Gere]. Ryan encouraged us to play. He approached it much more like an acting class or an acting exercise. It didn’t feel like a typical audition or a judgmental process. It wasn’t, “Are you good enough to play this part?” It was more, “Let’s play around, figure this out, and see how all of this feels.” Luckily, it all went well.
	
		Your narration is a big part of the show. How did you craft the character’s voice, and did you base it on Bret’s reading of the audiobook?	

	I wanted to use it as a reference, because it’s so interesting how people speak and what they choose to emphasize — where you can hear excitement and patterns like that. I found an interview with Bret in his early 20s, which was the closest I could find to what he would have sounded like in high school. I listened to that a bunch, and I worked with Ryan to make sure it wasn’t distracting, and that it was all in service of telling the story.
	
		Did you meet with Bret at any point? Has he been involved in your crafting of the character?	

	No. I mean, he’s been involved with the crafting of the character, but he’s been working with Ryan primarily. I’ve never gotten to meet him.
	
		Would it have been helpful to meet Bret, do you think? Or was it beneficial to have that distance?	

	I don’t know, just because I haven’t had that interaction. Just being able to focus on the scripts and lean on Ryan and what he was hoping to bring to life has maybe led to more clarity and was less overwhelming for me. I didn’t have access to Bret and I don’t have access to whatever information I could have potentially learned from that, so I could just let that piece go and really focus on what Ryan was giving us on the day.
	
	
		It’s interesting, because your part is both a real person and a fictional character.	

	That’s what’s so interesting about the book: So much of it is told with the phrase “I remember.” I remember I was driving on the Pacific Coast Highway. It’s almost like a motif in the text. I remember this, and I remember that. It’s all in retrospect, which is interesting to play. There’s a potential unreliable narrator element to it. Naturally, he is remembering a time that was very long ago, and we’re bringing that time period to life in the present.
	
		What was it like to film on location in L.A.? Sadly, that’s a rare thing these days.	

	It was so cool. It was insane to be listening to the book, driving the streets that he’s talking about — also commuting in L.A. for me was a first. I know the routes through the hills now way more intimately than I ever thought I would. It certainly made me feel like I finally do live here now. I can confidently navigate the city without a map — not that that’s ever a good idea, because you never know where traffic is going to show up. But L.A. is almost a character in the book, and I think the show is such a beautiful visual love letter to the city.
	
		There’s even a supposed secret shortcut to the Valley…	

	It exists, I think.
	
		Say more.	

	If Terry Schaffer has access to it, then it must be a real thing. No, I love the L.A.-specific Easter eggs, and the shot of Cielo Drive, and the references to the history of the city. There is so much myth that surrounds Los Angeles, and that’s what makes it feel so alive to be here — both in reality and in the show. It’s an almost mythical place. There’s an unreliable history about Los Angeles. Will we ever know if a lot of those tropes and references are true?
	
		Speaking of unreliability, so much of the book takes place in Bret’s head, and it’s unclear whether he is inventing certain things or actually seeing them. Plus, as you said, he’s recalling these events from decades later. How did you convey that unreliable factor on-screen, and how did you think about that while playing the part?	

	The way we bring that unreliability to life on screen is in the interactions between Bret and Robert. Some of those interactions happen only between them, with no witnesses. When they’re described to the group of friends by each character [after the fact], the descriptions are always different. We’re not sure who is lying and who is being truthful.
	
	
		The story requires a psychosexual relationship between Bret and Robert. How did you create that chemistry with Homer Gere?	

	That was something Ryan helped us with in the chemistry read. He encouraged us to play with the dynamics and find the buttons we could push on each other. What created a physical response, and how could I surprise Homer and try to throw him off in a scene? We played this interesting game of tennis. But also, Homer and I love each other so much, and we’ve spent so much time together. The chemistry is real, because we’re trying to push each other’s buttons, but there is this underlying smile of, “Man, you’re really good at this, and I love doing this with you.” Those were some of my favorite scenes to film.
	
		What were the most challenging scenes to film?	

	A big challenge actually came from how close we all got in real life. Bret has an interesting role in the friend group as this observer. He’s more connected to the world at large, and he’s starting to become isolated from his friends even though he cares deeply about them. He’s aware of all these happenings outside of their purview, and the more he tries to build a connection and reach out about the things that concern him, the less his friends want to entertain those conversations.

	The isolation was hard to play because we’d be in a scene together as a group of friends. As actors, we’re all friends and having the time of our lives, and I had to lock into this thing of “nobody is listening to me.” I’m remembering passages of voiceover in my head while everybody else is having a conversation around me, and I’m trying not to smile and join this group of lovely people that I adore spending time with.
	
		You could have gone Method, but then that would have been a more miserable experience.	

	I know. That definitely would have made some things easier, but then I would have missed out on so much!
	
		Your character, at least in the book, has quite a bit of sex. Was that something you thought about when auditioning? Did it make you nervous?	

	I definitely thought about it, but it wasn’t something I was very worried about. I wanted to make sure that I could pull it off in a way that was good for the screen and good for whatever aesthetic values Ryan had for the story. But I didn’t have any nerves about that. Obviously, we’re living in the time of intimacy coordinators, so all of it is carefully choreographed and specified and monitored. It’s like doing a dance under a microscope. It’s not a big cause for concern for me.
	
	
		There’s been a huge press blitz for “The Shards.” Over the past couple weeks you’ve been in New York, London, Berlin and Los Angeles. How does it feel to be No. 1 on the call sheet for a show like this?	

	I’ve had so many people, as they would say in “Lord of the Rings,” share the load with me. Ryan did a very special thing in creating this super tight cast. Everybody made us feel welcome and protected on set, and we had a little summer camp experience. It’s more unnerving that this experience I shared with a group of people I love is now being presented to the world. That’s a crazy trip. But I didn’t feel a ton of weight because everybody around me was so amazing. With the press tour, sometimes I felt a little bad because we were having so much fun with each other that maybe some of the questions weren’t given a satisfactory answer.

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘The Shards’ Star Igby Rigney on Wooing Ryan Murphy, Never Meeting Bret Easton Ellis and Not Worrying About Sex Scenes: ‘It’s Like Doing a Dance Under a Microscope’

title: Arizona Man Catches Fire After Federal Officer Deploys Taser at Gas Pump
description:
Arizona Man
                          Tased by Officer at Gas Pump, Bursts Into Flames
body:
Arizona Man
                          Tased by Officer at Gas Pump, Bursts Into Flames
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 5, 2026
                            5:52 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 5, 2026
                                8:23 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Arizona man's fishing trip ended with him literally going up in flames ... after a federal wildlife officer deployed a Taser while he was standing beside a gas pump.
      
    
            Clarence "Chuck" Coyl captured the absolutely terrifying July 16 confrontation on video at a gas station on the Fort Mojave Indian Reservation ... with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service officer pointing a Taser at him and demanding his ID.
      
    
            Coyl asks, "What am I being arrested for?" ... and the officer tells him he's not cooperating after committing a crime.
      
    
            That's when Coyl fires back, "A misdemeanor? A misdemeanor?" and starts to say, "It's a ten-dollar--" ... before the unmistakable crackle of the Taser cuts him off.
      

            Seconds later, Coyl's phone falls, flames erupt, and he can be heard shouting in pain.
      
    
            Coyl says the wild encounter began earlier at Havasu National Wildlife Refuge, where he and a friend planned to fish. According to Coyl, an officer accused the pair of trespassing and told them to leave ... so they did.
      
    
            He then encountered the same officer again at the gas station.
      
    
            Civil rights attorney Ben Crump later posted another jaw-dropping angle of the confrontation ... showing the officer extend the Taser toward Coyl beside the pickup and fuel pump before flames suddenly burst beneath the truck.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Coyl says he plans to take legal action after he suffered first and second-degree burns and nerve damage to two fingers ... and local reports say he has not been charged in connection with the encounter.
      
    
            U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service confirmed its officer deployed the Taser ... adding it had no further comment on the matter.
      
    
            Coyl went out looking to catch fish ... and wound up catching fire instead.

title: Donald Trump Jr. Pays Ex Kimberly Guilfoyle $7.6M to Buy Her Out of Florida Mansion
description:
Trump Jr. to Ex Kimberly Guilfoyle
                          Here's $7.6M, I'll Take the House!!!
body:
Trump Jr. to Ex Kimberly Guilfoyle
                          Here's $7.6M, I'll Take the House!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 5, 2026
                            5:33 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Donald Trump Jr. is officially cutting one of the last big financial ties to ex-fiancée Kimberly Guilfoyle ... shelling out $7.6 Million to buy her out of the Florida mansion they once shared.
      
    
            According to a deed filed Monday and reported by The Palm Beach Post, Don Jr. paid Guilfoyle the hefty sum for her share of their waterfront estate in Jupiter's ultra-exclusive Admirals Cove community ... with the deal closing July 25.
      
    
            The former couple bought the sprawling pad together for $9.7 Million in 2021, back when they were still very much an item. The place clocks in at more than 11,000 square feet with 6 bedrooms and 11 bathrooms ... plus a pool, private dock, elevator, and plenty of waterfront views.
      

            Don Jr. and Kimberly's engagement quietly ended in 2024 after years together. And, while there was no divorce -- they never actually married -- Don Jr. has certainly moved on ... he said "I do" to Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in May.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Meanwhile, Kimberly has moved on geographically, too ... she's now serving as the U.S. ambassador to Greece.
      
    
            So, Don Jr.'s got a new wife and now full control of the old house ... but officially closing the book on this particular chapter didn't come cheap.

title: Man Dressed as Grim Reaper Arrested for Staring at Patients From Hospital Roof
description:
Man Dressed as Grim Reaper
                          Arrested for Staring Down Hospital Patients
body:
Man Dressed as Grim Reaper
                          Arrested for Staring Down Hospital Patients From Roof
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A hospital is usually where people go to avoid the Grim Reaper ... not find him waiting on the roof.
      
    
            A man named Leon Gillespie -- decked out in a black hooded costume and carrying what appeared to be a long scythe -- took his scare act to new heights June 6 ... climbing atop Ysbyty Glan Clwyd hospital in North Wales.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Cops and firefighters rushed to the scene ... and Gillespie remained on the roof for roughly 50 minutes -- even making noises at the people on the ground -- until police eventually brought him down. He was charged with causing a nuisance or disturbance on National Health Service property.
      

            Here’s the real twist ... Gillespie insisted he wasn't dressed as the Grim Reaper at all -- he claimed the costume was supposed to be a bird or crow.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He pleaded guilty to the nuisance charge July 15 and was fined £200.
      
    
            Apparently, the hospital stunt wasn't his only recent offense, either ... Gillespie also reportedly admitted stealing cat food and litter from a pet store in March, along with food and drinks from a supermarket in May.
      
    
            In the end ... the only thing this Reaper reaped was trouble.

title: Lauryn Hill Draws Huge Crowd for Fugees Anniversary Celebration
description:
Lauryn Hill
                          Draws Thousands to Fugees Pop-Up
body:
Lauryn Hill
                          Draws Thousands to Fugees Pop-Up
                      
      
    
            Lauryn Hill joined Wyclef Jean for a Fugees' album anniversary celebration ... and thousands turned out to get a peek at the superstar.
      
    
            Lauryn and Wyclef gave fans a thrill at Piccadilly Circus ... taking snaps and signing albums to celebrate the release of their iconic album "The Score."
      
    
            It's all part of the promotional run for a full-album performance Friday at the Diaspora Calling! festival.
      
    
            Lauryn gave major props to acclaimed Los Angeles artist Lauren Halsey ... who was commissioned to paint a mural for the celebration.
      
    
            One thing's for sure ... Lauryn is still killing them softly!!!
